      Doing Good by Loading Historical Data to eBird

      Home 2026 August 11 Doing Good by Loading Historical Data to eBird

      feel free to call us    765-205-1255     Contact Us

      Listen to audio version of this article
      Sponsored by
      0:00 / 10:46
      Instaread

      Image: An eBird checklist showing historical bird records from April 27, 1881, at Monteur’s Pond in Knox County, as documented by Robert Ridgway and published in Amos Butler’s 1898 The Birds of Indiana. This data, now part of the Amos Butler Data account on eBird, represents the kind of digitized historical records that Bob Guth continues to add to eBird.

      BY ROBERT W. GUTH

      As a Mennonite, I always like helping others, which is a strong tradition for us. As an introvert with an autism diagnosis, I prefer working by myself. After my PhD, I taught at Goshen College for two years, but I quickly decided that I did not like such a social job. I then found a new job as a beginning actuary at Mennonite Mutual Aid (now Everence Financial), and I stayed for 31 years. I did have biology and mathematic majors in college, so the career change is not as strange as it may seem. Now in retirement, I walk and watch birds every morning, and I load historical bird data into spreadsheets for eBird for much of the rest of the day when I can.

      I opened an eBird account in October 2011. For two years beginning in December 2012, I worked on evenings and weekends to load my life’s bird records into eBird. They dated from 1961 to 1999 for the most part. Since I love detail and persistence, I put the records into spreadsheets and uploaded them to eBird. By the time I finished two years later, it was over 490 spreadsheets. I continued birding on vacations, and a trip to Colorado led to the Colorado eBird Hotspot editor to suggest to eBird that I become the Indiana eBird Hotspot editor, which I still do.

      Indiana had about 200 Hotspots when I started as Hotspot editor but now has over 1800. My hotspot work led me to visit all 92 Indiana counties with my wife. I especially liked visiting Ohio, Switzerland, and Tipton Counties, all of which had fewer than 150 eBird checklists at that time. We saw a Worm-eating Warbler in Switzerland County, and now dozens of birders visit that county.

      One’s eBird account normally receives bird observations either by using data entry on a webpage, or by using the eBird app on a phone. However, historical data and other bulk data can be uploaded in a spreadsheet. This is a fast method. The Checklist format can take up to 48 columns of data for 48 checklists, and the record format can take a horizontal-format spreadsheet with up to almost 5,000 lines of data. Both methods process the upload in two to four minutes usually. I have used both spreadsheet methods a lot.

      In retirement, after a birding trip to 10 islands of the Lesser Antilles in the Caribbean, I got the idea to go through my 25 years of James Bond’s Supplement to the Checklist of the Birds of the West Indies, and to extract the bird records to eBird that had enough detail to do so. Jeff Gerbracht, then at eBird, helped me understand how to do that, as he is a West Indies regional eBird editor. He encouraged me to add museum specimen numbers when I could find them. That project plus finding old publication data and loading 30 years of mist net bird results from Puerto Rico, lasted throughout 2024.

      My appetite to play detective and get more data brought me to my two current large eBird projects. One was a volunteer project to help staff at Illinois Natural History Survey digitize and load to eBird their older bird data. I worked there as a summer field assistant in summers of 1967 to 1969. I had the joy of loading data from my former boss (now deceased) to eBird, as well as a lot of other data. That project continues as they dig old, detailed records out of their archives.

      My other large volunteer project is in Indiana. I had birded with Kenneth J. Brock and others on Saturdays from 2014 to 2019, and I knew that he kept a database of Indiana bird records, but he did not use eBird. Many years ago, I asked Brad Bumgardner what would replace Ken after he died, and Brad said, “eBird.” After Ken died, I waited patiently, but I then heard that Indiana Audubon needed someone to access the database and translate it for use outside a Macintosh operating system. I learned that my Goshen friend Leland Shaum was receiving quarterly updates of the database to use to obtain data for the Amish-related bird publication, The Michiana Meadowlark. Leland had permission from Ken to use the database widely as long as Ken was given credit. Leland was able to provide me with Mac files of the data, and after 40 days of work, I had five spreadsheets of 3.2 million records of bird data that were from the Kenneth J. Brock Indiana Bird Database.

      Now I have been enjoying loading Brock data to eBird. Over half of the records came from eBird, so my current work is only 1.44 million records. First, I loaded all of the Ken Brock personal sightings to a Ken Brock account. It was three days and about eight hours of uploads, after a week or two of preparation. The Kenneth J. Brock eBird account now has 369 species and 27,925 checklists dating from 1970 to 2023. I then helped a couple of Ken’s fellow birders add to their eBird records, with many records that predated their eBird accounts (like 1990 to 2014).

      Moving records from the Brock database to eBird has several significant nuances. First, I need data with an exact date, location, observer, and species count. Sometimes Ken had only a county location and no observer name. Searching back into source publications often clears that up, but sometimes a record needs to be left unused due to lack of information.

      Second, I needed to decide which eBird accounts the data goes into. Ken’s personal observations went into the Kenneth J. Brock eBird account. Many other birder observations, such as my own, were already on eBird, and I did not want to create duplicate entries. I am planning for an Amos Butler Data account for observations cited by Amos Butler in The Birds of Indiana, 1898. There will be a Ken Brock Data account for other bird records from various birders, mostly prior to 1970. The Data word as last name means that there are many different observers, and that account does not go into the top 100. There will be a Russell Mumford account for his observations, and maybe a Mumford Keller Data account for observations cited in The Birds of Indiana (1984) by Russell Mumford and Charles Keller. I am still deciding what to do with the James Haw records, which are a large number, but only a few are in his account on eBird.

      Third, the Ken Brock Database lists almost 2000 bird specimens, so I downloaded data on 2000 Indiana bird specimens from the Smithsonian, another 1,000 Indiana specimens from the Field Museum, and many more from the Joseph Moore Museum at Earlham College, the Chicago Academy of Science, and the Indiana State Museum. I intend to add specimen numbers to Ken’s records when I can match the dates and collectors, and maybe also add additional museum records to eBird that are not in Ken’s database. This will provide a good base of older bird record data to eBird from Indiana.

      Most recently, I have been working with bird records dated before 1900. As a scientist, I prefer detail and want exact records as much as possible. Many of Ken’s pre-1900 data have general locations, but more exact locations could be found in the literature sources that Ken cited. I have found hundreds of additional records with locations by looking at sources like Amos Butler, The Birds of Indiana, 1898. I am using those as much as I can, since these are already published records. My friends in Illinois want as much data as possible from old migration dates so that they can compare with current patterns that may be changing with the climate.

      Here are three examples of how I enjoy this detective work. Records in Butler, 1898, talked about birds at Edwards, Indiana, in Vigo County, by a particular birder. I found no Edwards, Indiana, in Google Maps. After a long search in Google, I determined that Edwards was a rail station name in Vigo County, and I located it in a 27-page document of rail stations in Indiana. It was where I expected at North Terre Haute. Another example was Yellow-crowned Night Herons at Monteur’s Pond eight miles east of Vincennes. Google Maps had no pond. I finally found the Pond in an 1890 map image from the state library. It was a wetland that was drained and is now farm fields with one or two straight ditches in it. This gives me the exact location, however. A final example was a Black Rail record in 1894 in Putnam County. This rare bird was seen on two days but would not fly so it could not be shot as a specimen. That was the standard for identification in 1894. It was then found three days later at the same marsh by birders with a dog, but it would not fly. On the fourth try, the dog caught a juvenile Black Rail and an adult. This provided two specimens and proof of breeding. The effort to catch the rails took a full week. The specimens are in the Smithsonian, and I have the specimen numbers for the eBird record.

      I anticipate my work on the Brock Database to take another six to 24 months. With my emphasis on detail, knowledge of eBird Hotspots, and a lifetime of watching birds and working with spreadsheets, this work with historic data is a great fit for me. I am confident that the data will be useful for many others.

      Robert W. Guth has a PhD in Biology where the thesis was a study of Chicago urban birds. He is also a retired actuary (FSA, MAAA CERA) of Everence Financial, a Mennonite-related fraternal benefit society and insurance company. Bob is a member of Indiana Audubon, American Ornithological Society, and a life member of the Wilson Ornithological Society. Since 2015, he has been the Indiana eBird Hotspot editor. Bob tries to help with 7 Christmas Bird Counts annually, and formerly the Breeding Bird Survey and Sandhill Crane counts for the DNR were his annual tasks. Bob’s wife, Christine, uses eBird, but mostly is a botany expert.

      WE BELIEVE

      Indiana Audubon Society believes strongly in making birding a safe and accessible activity for all people, regardless of race, color, gender, national origin, age, religion, creed, disability, veteran’s status, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression.

      We believe continuing efforts, discussions and action, no matter how uncomfortable at times, are needed to further ensure that birding and nature enjoyment is safe and accessible for everyone. We pledge to continue to support those that share our values and strive to make the outdoors truly accessible for everyone.

      About Us

      Indiana Audubon Society's mission is to engage communities in the enjoyment of birds in their habitat, through conservation, education, and research.
